deal in.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: the habitual trade sense (*the gallery deals in prints*) and the one-time card sense (*deal me in*). No linking or stative use.
deal in.passive: **restricted** — the card sense passivizes: *I was dealt in on the second hand*. The trade sense barely does: ✗ *nineteenth-century prints are dealt in by the gallery*.

deal out.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: handing out cards or portions, and administering a penalty. Progressive is normal — *he's dealing out the cards*.
deal out.passive: **yes** — *the estate was dealt out among four cousins*; *the same sentence is dealt out for a first offense*.

deal with.verb type: action — dynamic in the handling and business senses (*I'm dealing with vendor complaints*), but **stative** in the be-about sense: ✗ *chapter four is dealing with the war years*.
deal with.passive: **restricted** — full prepositional passive in the handling and business senses: *the complaint has already been dealt with*. The be-about sense resists it: ✗ *the war years are dealt with by chapter four*.

dig in.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: starting to eat, entrenching, and the *dig in one's heels* idiom. Progressive is normal — *management has been digging in for weeks*.
dig in.passive: **no** — the eating and entrenching senses take no object at all, and the one object it does take resists the passive: ✗ *her heels were dug in*.

dig into.verb type: action — dynamic: investigating, tucking into food, drawing on savings. Progressive is common — *she has been digging into the family's history*.
dig into.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is marginal even in the investigate sense: ?*his campaign filings were dug into for weeks*. None at all in the food and savings senses: ✗ *savings were dug into*.

dig out.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: retrieving something stored away, and freeing something buried.
dig out.passive: **yes** — *the warranty was dug out and emailed over*; *two cars were dug out of the drift*.

dig up.verb type: action — dynamic: unearthing facts, producing something with effort, or turning over ground.
dig up.passive: **yes** — *an old lawsuit was dug up by opposition researchers*; *the whole yard was dug up looking for the leak*.

do away with.verb type: action — dynamic in both the abolish sense and the dated kill sense. Progressive is fine — *they're doing away with paper permits*.
do away with.passive: **yes**, and the entry shows it — *the rule has been done away with twice and brought back twice*. The particle chain stays intact after the verb.

do for.verb type: action — dynamic in the British active sense (*that hill did for me*); the American survival, *be done for*, is a fixed participle used adjectivally, i.e. stative.
do for.passive: **restricted** — no true passive of the active verb (✗ *the pipes were done for by two winters*). Only the adjectival participle lives on: *if the bank calls the loan, we're done for*.

do in.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, exhausting someone and killing someone. The participle *done in* also serves as an adjective: *I'm done in*.
do in.passive: **yes** — *the witness was done in before the trial*; *half the crew was done in by the heat*.

do out of.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of cheating someone. Progressive is fine — *they're doing her out of her share*.
do out of.passive: **yes**, with the person cheated as subject — *she was done out of her share of the house*. The thing lost cannot front: ✗ *her commission was done her out of*.

do over.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: redoing a task, redecorating a room, and British burgling or beating up.
do over.passive: **yes** — *the essay had to be done over*; *the kitchen was done over in the spring*; *their flat got done over while they were away*.

do up.verb type: action — dynamic: fastening, wrapping, renovating. The participle *done up* doubles as an adjective — *she showed up done up like it was a wedding*.
do up.passive: **yes** — *the package was done up in brown paper*; *the house was done up over two summers*.

do with.verb type: **stative** in both fixed frames — *could do with* is a want or need and *have to do with* is a relation: ✗ *I am doing with a coffee*, ✗ *the delay is having nothing to do with the weather*. Only *what to do with* is dynamic.
do with.passive: **no** — both frames are fixed and take no passive: ✗ *a cup of coffee could be done with*, ✗ *the weather is had nothing to do with*.

do without.verb type: action — dynamic, an ongoing managing rather than a state: *we're doing without a car this year* is fine. Works with an object or with none at all.
do without.passive: **no** — ✗ *a car was done without for two years*. The object stays after the preposition, and the objectless use has nothing to passivize.

draw back.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: the physical recoil and the pulling out of a commitment.
draw back.passive: **no** — the verb takes no object in either sense, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the merger was drawn back from*.

draw down.verb type: action — dynamic: reducing a reserve by using it. Progressive is standard in finance writing — *they're drawing down the credit line in stages*.
draw down.passive: **yes**, and the entry shows it — *inventories have been drawn down faster than the plants can refill them*.

draw in.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: attracting people, the shortening of daylight, and a train arriving.
draw in.passive: **yes** in the attract sense — *thousands of subscribers were drawn in by a free first month*. No passive of the daylight or train senses, which take no object.

draw on.verb type: action — dynamic: dipping into a resource (*she's drawing on her savings*), and in the literary time sense (*as the evening drew on*).
draw on.passive: **restricted** — the resource sense takes a prepositional passive in careful writing: *the emergency fund was drawn on twice that year*. The time sense has no object and no passive.

draw out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: prolonging, coaxing someone into talking, and withdrawing money.
draw out.passive: **yes**, and the entry shows it — *the negotiation was drawn out over eleven months*; *the shyest kid in the room was drawn out*.

draw up.verb type: action — dynamic: preparing a document, a vehicle pulling to a stop, or straightening to full height in *draw oneself up*.
draw up.passive: **yes** in the document sense — *the lease was drawn up in an afternoon*. No passive of the vehicle sense (no object) or of the reflexive: ✗ *he was drawn up by himself*.

dream of.verb type: **stative** — a mental state of longing rather than an act, though it takes the progressive with a temporary reading: *she's been dreaming of a year off*. The negative *wouldn't dream of* is a fixed frame.
dream of.passive: **no** — ✗ *a year with nothing scheduled is dreamed of by her*. Only the attributive participle survives: *a long dreamed-of promotion*.

dream on.verb type: action — dynamic in form, but frozen as a bare imperative retort; it has essentially no tensed paradigm beyond *they can dream on*.
dream on.passive: **no** — the verb takes no object at all, so there is no passive: ✗ *it was dreamed on*.

dream up.verb type: action — dynamic: a single act of invention. Progressive is fine — *marketing is dreaming up a new name*.
dream up.passive: **yes** — *the whole seating chart was dreamed up in an afternoon*; *the conspiracy had been dreamed up in one sleepless night*.

drink away.verb type: action — dynamic: spending or dispelling money, time, or grief by drinking.
drink away.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but rare, since the active is what people say: ?*most of the inheritance was drunk away inside a year*. A diagnosis cannot be: ✗ *a diagnosis can't be drunk away* is odd outside a joke.

drink in.verb type: action — dynamic: taking in a view or applause with pleasure. Progressive is normal — *they were drinking in the view*.
drink in.passive: **restricted** — the passive is stiff and rarely worth using: ?*the applause was drunk in*. The active carries this verb.

drink to.verb type: action — dynamic: the single act of raising a glass.
drink to.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive does not work here: ✗ *the newlyweds were drunk to*. Only the fixed reply *I'll drink to that* keeps the object out front, and that is not a passive.

drink up.verb type: action — dynamic, most often the bare imperative, which takes no object at all: *drink up, we're leaving*.
drink up.passive: **restricted** — possible with a full object (*every drop of the lemonade was drunk up*) but rare; the imperative use has nothing to passivize.

drive at.verb type: action — dynamic, and effectively locked in the progressive: *what are you driving at?*, ✗ *what do you drive at?*
drive at.passive: **no** — ✗ *what is being driven at by you?* The object stays after the preposition, usually as the question word.

drive away.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: repelling people and simply leaving by car.
drive away.passive: **yes** in the repel sense — *half the regulars were driven away by the new prices*. No passive of the depart sense, which takes no object.

drive down.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing a price or a rate lower. Progressive is standard — *cheap imports are driving down the price of steel*.
drive down.passive: **yes**, and the entry shows it — *wholesale prices have been driven down to 2019 levels*.

drive home.verb type: action — dynamic: making a point land by repetition or evidence.
drive home.passive: **yes**, and the entry shows it — *say it again until it's driven home*; *the point was driven home by the photographs*.

drive off.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: repelling, leaving by car, and the golf tee shot.
drive off.passive: **yes** in the repel sense — *the coyotes were driven off twice that week*. No passive of the depart sense, which takes no object.

drive out.verb type: action — dynamic: forcing someone out of a place or a market.
drive out.passive: **yes**, and the entry shows it — *the occupying force was finally driven out in the spring*; *families were driven out of the neighborhood by rent increases*.

drive up.verb type: action — dynamic: pushing a price or a number higher, or pulling up in a vehicle.
drive up.passive: **yes** in the push-higher sense — *land values have been driven up fourfold*. No passive of the pull-up sense, which takes no object.

eat away at.verb type: action — dynamic, and typically progressive to show the slow wear: *inflation has been eating away at their savings*.
eat away at.passive: **restricted** — the three-part chain passivizes stiffly: ?*the foundation has been eaten away at by salt water*. Writers drop the *at* instead: *the underside was eaten away*.

eat in.verb type: action — dynamic: having the meal at home. Progressive is normal — *we're eating in tonight*.
eat in.passive: **no** — the verb takes no object at all, so there is no passive: ✗ *dinner was eaten in*.

eat into.verb type: action — dynamic: consuming part of a fund, a margin, or a schedule. Progressive is common — *returns are eating into the margin*.
eat into.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is marginal at best: ?*the vacation fund was eaten into by the repairs*. The active is what gets written.

eat out.verb type: action — dynamic: taking the meal at a restaurant.
eat out.passive: **no** — the verb takes no object at all: ✗ *dinner was eaten out*. (*He hasn't eaten out since the diagnosis* is a perfect, not a passive.)

eat up.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: finishing food, consuming a resource, lapping something up, and the passive-only *be eaten up with*.
eat up.passive: **yes** — *the settlement was eaten up by legal fees*; *the whole pan was eaten up before dinner*. Sense 4 exists only as a passive: *she's eaten up with jealousy*.

fall apart.verb type: action — dynamic, a process verb; the progressive is natural for the slow senses (*their marriage has been falling apart for years*).
fall apart.passive: **no** — intransitive in all three senses, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the binder was fallen apart*, ✗ *the deal was fallen apart over one clause*.

fall back.verb type: action — dynamic, a movement verb: literal with troops and crowds, figurative with numbers (*sales fell back after the holidays*).
fall back.passive: **no** — no object at all: ✗ *the second ridge was fallen back to*. Only the separate verb *fall back on* takes anything.

fall back on.verb type: action — dynamic; the act of resorting to something when the first option fails (*the report fell back on anecdotes*), not a state.
fall back on.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is grammatical but strained: ?*the same three jokes were fallen back on all night*. Americans recast with *resort to* or *rely on*.

fall behind.verb type: action — dynamic; a gradual process, comfortable in the progressive (*production has been falling behind all quarter*).
fall behind.passive: **no** — *behind* stays a preposition of position and will not promote: ✗ *the rest of the class was fallen behind by him*, ✗ *the mortgage was fallen behind on*.

fall down.verb type: action — dynamic; a body or a structure dropping in sense 1, an argument that stops working in sense 2 (*the plan falls down on cost*).
fall down.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the last three steps were fallen down*, ✗ *follow-up has been fallen down on*.

fall for.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses; each names an event, not a state — *he fell for her the first week of the job*.
fall for.passive: **no** — ✗ *the same email was fallen for by thousands*, ✗ *she was fallen for*. Use *be taken in by* for the trick sense.

fall in.verb type: action — dynamic; a collapse in sense 1, a maneuver in sense 2, where it is usually an order (*Fall in — two ranks, on the road*).
fall in.passive: **no** — neither sense takes an object: ✗ *the tunnel was fallen in*, ✗ *the platoon was fallen in before dawn*.

fall in with.verb type: action — dynamic; both senses name something that happens at a point in time — meeting a crowd, or coming around to a plan.
fall in with.passive: **no** — ✗ *a bad crowd was fallen in with*, ✗ *the plan was fallen in with without much argument*. Recast as *took up with* or *went along with*.

fall off.verb type: action — dynamic; a gradual decline in sense 1 (*quality has been falling off*), a single event in sense 2 (*the handle fell off*).
fall off.passive: **no** — intransitive; what follows the literal *fall off* belongs to the preposition: ✗ *the ladder was fallen off*.

fall on.verb type: **stative** in the date and duty senses — a standing fact, ✗ *Christmas is falling on a Tuesday*; **action** (dynamic) in the attack sense, *they fell on the food*.
fall on.passive: **restricted** — only the attack sense, and it reads literary: *the wagons were fallen on before dawn*. ✗ *a Tuesday is fallen on by Christmas*, ✗ *the tenant is fallen on by the cost*.

fall out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: quarreling, hair or screws coming loose, a company leaving formation.
fall out.passive: **no** — intransitive; the person you quarrel with is the object of *with*, not of the verb: ✗ *her business partner was fallen out with*.

fall through.verb type: action — dynamic; an event, the collapse of an arrangement before it can happen (*the sale fell through two days before closing*).
fall through.passive: **no** — intransitive, no object: ✗ *the sale was fallen through*, ✗ *the financing was fallen through*.

fall under.verb type: **stative** in the classifying sense — a standing fact, ✗ *the site is falling under federal jurisdiction*; dynamic when it names a change of hands (*the department fell under her control after the merger*).
fall under.passive: **no** — ✗ *petty cash is fallen under by anything under fifty dollars*, ✗ *HR is fallen under by those complaints*. Say *is covered by* or *comes under*.

feed back.verb type: action — dynamic; a transfer of information, mechanical (*the sensors feed back readings every second*) or human (*she fed back two pages of notes*).
feed back.passive: **yes** — *the output is fed back into the input*, which is where the noun *feedback* comes from; *the survey results were fed back to the team on Friday*.

feed into.verb type: action — dynamic; a continuing contribution, at home in the progressive (*his resentment had been feeding into every meeting for a year*).
feed into.passive: **no** — ✗ *the same problem is fed into by every complaint*, ✗ *the panic is fed into by coverage like that*. (The literal *the paper is fed into the printer* is a different pattern, with a direct object.)

feed off.verb type: action — dynamic; taking food or energy over time, and the progressive is normal (*she's been feeding off other people's work for years*).
feed off.passive: **no** — ✗ *the crowd is fed off by him*, ✗ *people's fear of missing out is fed off*. Recast active, or use *live off of*.

feed on.verb type: action — dynamic; habitual eating in sense 1, a continuing process in sense 2 (*panic had fed on rumor for a week*).
feed on.passive: **no** — ✗ *insects are fed on by bats*, ✗ *silence is fed on by suspicion*. The natural *the dog was fed on scraps* belongs to the other pattern, where *the dog* is the direct object.

feed up.verb type: action — dynamic in the fatten sense; the fixed *be fed up (with)* is **stative** — a state of exasperation, ✗ *I am being fed up with the excuses*.
feed up.passive: **yes** — *they sent her to the coast to be fed up after the illness*, and the everyday American form exists only in passive shape: *I'm fed up with the excuses*, *she got fed up and quit*.

feel for.verb type: **stative** in the sympathy sense — a feeling, not an act (*I really feel for her*); **action** (dynamic) in the grope sense, where the progressive is normal: *she was feeling for the edge of the step*.
feel for.passive: **no** — ✗ *she was felt for by everyone*, ✗ *the light switch was felt for in the dark*. Do not confuse it with *feel up*, which passivizes freely.

feel like.verb type: **stative** in both senses — a mood in sense 1 (✗ *I am feeling like a nap*) and a perception in sense 2, where *feel* is **linking**: *it feels like November out there*.
feel like.passive: **no** — stative perception, and *like* is a preposition rather than an object marker: ✗ *a nap is felt like*, ✗ *three hours was felt like by that meeting*.

feel out.verb type: action — dynamic; deliberate probing, fine in the progressive (*they're feeling the market out with a small run*).
feel out.passive: **yes** — *he hadn't been felt out about the job before the offer went in*; *two of the partners were felt out over lunch*.

feel up.verb type: action — dynamic; a physical act, and it takes the progressive: *he was feeling her up on the train*.
feel up.passive: **yes**, and the passive is how the complaint is usually worded — *nobody should have to worry about being felt up on the way to work*.

feel up to.verb type: **stative** — a state of readiness rather than an act (*he hasn't felt up to much since the surgery*); the progressive shows up only in the softened *I'm not feeling up to it today*.
feel up to.passive: **no** — ✗ *a three-hour drive isn't felt up to*, ✗ *another round of interviews wasn't felt up to by anyone*. The complement stays after *to*.

fight back.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: retaliating in sense 1, pushing an emotion down in sense 2 (*he fought back tears through the whole eulogy*).
fight back.passive: **restricted** — only sense 2, and it reads bookish: *the tears were fought back until the car door closed*. Sense 1 takes no object at all: ✗ *it was fought back by the union*.

fight down.verb type: action — dynamic; the deliberate suppression of a feeling as it rises, commonest in narrative past (*she fought her panic down and finished the presentation*).
fight down.passive: **restricted** — grammatical, with the feeling as subject — *the urge was fought down and nothing was said* — but rare; American writing keeps this one active.

fight off.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: repelling an attacker, holding off an illness, beating back a rival.
fight off.passive: **yes** — *the raiders had been fought off twice before*; *two primary challengers were fought off*; *a cold that can't be fought off with coffee*.

fight out.verb type: action — dynamic; settling a dispute by carrying it through to a finish, usually with the near-empty object *it* (*let them fight it out*).
fight out.passive: **restricted** — fine with a real object, *the last two seats were fought out in court*, but the ordinary *fight it out* has no passive: ✗ *it was fought out by the two departments*.

find for.verb type: action — dynamic; a courtroom act, the moment a verdict is returned (*the jury found for the plaintiff on all four counts*).
find for.passive: **no** — ✗ *the plaintiff was found for*, ✗ *the city was found against*. Court reporting says *judgment was entered for the plaintiff* instead.

find out.verb type: action — dynamic; the event of knowledge arriving (*we'll find out on Thursday*), not a state like *know*.
find out.passive: **yes** — strongest in the expose sense: *sooner or later he'll be found out*, *nobody knew, and she was never found out*. Also *the layoffs were found out about within a day*.

fit in.verb type: action — dynamic in the scheduling sense (*she fit two more errands in before noon*); closer to **stative** in the belong sense, a standing fact about a person: *he never really fit in at that school*.
fit in.passive: **restricted** — only the scheduling sense, and it is ordinary office talk: *I was fit in between two other appointments*. The belong sense has no object: ✗ *that school was never fit in*.

fit in with.verb type: **stative** — compatibility, a standing relation rather than an act; the progressive is odd: ✗ *Tuesday is fitting in with your schedule*.
fit in with.passive: **no** — one of the *fit / suit / match* group that refuses the passive even with something after it: ✗ *your schedule is fit in with by Tuesday*, ✗ *the model isn't fit in with by her findings*.

fit out.verb type: action — dynamic; the work of equipping a place, a vehicle, or a crew (*they fit out the whole clinic for under a hundred thousand*).
fit out.passive: **yes**, and the passive is at least as common as the active — *the schooner was fitted out for a two-year voyage*, *every truck gets fitted out with a second radio*.

fit up.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: framing someone in sense 1, equipping a place in sense 2.
fit up.passive: **yes** — *he always claimed he'd been fitted up by the squad*; *the gym was fitted up with donated equipment*.

fly at.verb type: action — dynamic; a sudden attack, an event (*she flew at him before anyone could stand up*).
fly at.passive: **no** — ✗ *the mailman was flown at by the dog*, ✗ *the referee was flown at*. Say *went after him* or *lunged at him*.

fly by.verb type: action — dynamic; time passing in sense 1 (*the summer flew by*), literal speed in sense 2 (*a motorcycle flew by on the shoulder*).
fly by.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the summer was flown by*, ✗ *the window was flown by*.

fly out.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses; note that the baseball sense is regular — *he flied out to right field*, never ✗ *he flew out to right field*.
fly out.passive: **restricted** — only the dispatch sense: *two engineers were flown out the same night*, *he was flown out to Phoenix for the interview*. ✗ *Newark is flown out of at six*, and the baseball sense has no object at all.

forget about.verb type: action — dynamic; a change of mental state (*I completely forgot about the dentist*), unlike stative *know*; sense 2 lives mostly in the imperative.
forget about.passive: **yes** — one of the few prepositional verbs here with a clean passive: *the crate had been forgotten about in the basement*, *the whole argument was forgotten about by Monday*.

freeze out.verb type: action — dynamic; a campaign of exclusion carried out over time (*they didn't fire her; they just froze her out*).
freeze out.passive: **yes** — *he was frozen out of every meeting that mattered*; *the two founders were frozen out by the majority owners*.

freeze over.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state (*the pond freezes over by early January most years*).
freeze over.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is no verbal passive: ✗ *the pond was frozen over by the cold*. *The lake is frozen over* is the adjective describing the result, not something done to the lake.

freeze up.verb type: action — dynamic, a change of state in both senses: a person going blank, a pipe or a lock seizing with cold.
freeze up.passive: **no** — intransitive: ✗ *the pipes were frozen up by the holiday cold*. After *be*, *frozen up* is an adjective naming the state, not a passive.
